newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president rejects state of emergency call.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president rejects state of emergency call.

text.p: Troops were deployed around Albania on Monday after a weekend of violent protests, and the ruling right-wing Democrats called for a counter-demonstration against rival Socialists they accuse of stoking the unrest.
Despite the unrest, President Sali Berisha said he saw no need to call a state of emergency as urged to do by Albania's parliament, mostly made up of his Democrats.

"The President of the Republic Sali Berisha refused to establish a full or partial state of emergency in the country," the president's office said in a statement. "He made it known to parliament that he would not accept such a thing."
The president said troops would only be used for a limited period to replace police officers injured in demonstrations, the statement said.
It did not specify how long troops would be deployed.
Berisha assumed special powers on Sunday to try to calm the biggest crisis of his five-year rule and head off further protests.

In Tirana, armed soldiers surrounded the central bank and guarded state television headquarters after Sunday's clashes in the capital, a prison riot and waves of demonstrations mainly in the south of the Balkan state.
Seven army trucks were seen on Monday evening parked around the Defence Ministry on central Skanderbeg Square, where protesters battled with riot police on Sunday.
Radio Tirana said soldiers had begun clearing roads near weekend flashpoints where protesters had erected barricades of rocks to prevent police reinforcements reaching their towns.

Troops had cleared one road near the town of Memaliaj, 190 km (120 miles) south of Tirana but the radio said units were still attempting to unblock the main route between Rrogozhine and Lushnje, where protesters hurled rocks at police on Saturday and physically attacked Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu.
In an atmosphere of growing anarchy, two inmates were killed in a riot and failed breakout at a prison in central Albania late on Sunday.
Prison officials said security had been stepped up at jails around the country but they would not hesitate to call in the army if trouble got out of control.
The wave of unrest has been sparked by growing anger over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in which Albanians have poured billions of leks (millions of dollars) in cash.
Thousands turned to violence when two of nine national schemes closed down, leaving some families destitute and others fearing their investments in other funds could also disappear.

Opposition parties, which boycotted general elections last May after accusing the Democrats of vote-rigging, have demanded Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government resign over its handling of the pyramid schemes and called for new polls.
The opposition has also accused the Democrats of using the schemes to finance general and local election campaigns last year, a charge rejected as "vile slander" by the government.
The World Bank and International Monetary Fund have urged Tirana to impose strict controls on so-called pyramid schemes.
The Democrats went on the offensive on Monday, calling for a peaceful counter-demonstration on Tuesday outside Socialist Party headquarters just off Skanderbeg Square.
Foreign Minister Shehu, the Democratic Party chairman, told hundreds of supporters that left-wingers were to blame for provoking two weeks of protests.
"I invite you to gather tomorrow in front of Socialist Party headquarters...to protest peacefully against the leaders of this party," Shehu told some 700 chanting supporters.

Such a gathering was likely to inflame an already tense atmosphere, but the Democrats are intent on flexing their muscles after seeing many of their party offices torched in weekend demonstrations in the south.
